title: Four curves, two edges
intro: The level above names the four statistics and the two depths they agree on. This level takes them one at a time: what quantity is actually computed, over what, why the shape of each curve licenses the boundary read off it, and where a curve moves for reasons that belong to the lens rather than to the model.

chapters.title: One instrument, four questions
chapters.body:
All four curves in [[fig-28]] are read through the same operation. The [[jacobian-lens]] reads a layer with a single matrix multiply: for a residual-stream state $h_\ell$, the [[j-lens-readout]] is $\text{lens}(h_\ell) = \text{softmax}(W_U\,\text{norm}(J_\ell h_\ell))$, where $J_\ell$ is that layer's [[averaged-jacobian]] and $W_U$ the model's [[unembedding-matrix]]. The output is one score for every token in the vocabulary.

Three of the four statistics are functions of that score vector. Each is computed at a single position and layer, then pooled over a large set of activations recorded on real text.

The fourth touches no activations at all. It is a property of the layer's dictionary — the [[j-lens-vector]]s, the rows of $W_U J_\ell$, one per vocabulary token — and asks how widely those vectors are spread through the [[residual-stream]]. A layer can score low on it for reasons that have nothing to do with what any particular activation holds.

The four also do not each mark both edges. Kurtosis and dimensionality are read for the onset. Next-token accuracy is read for the offset. Autocorrelation is the only one whose curve is used at both ends.

None of them comes with a stated threshold. Each is a curve, and a boundary is the depth at which its slope changes. The curves are sampled at twenty-five depths ([[layer-subsampling]]), so an inflection is being read off a coarse grid.

The argument of [[workspace-boundary-metrics]] is therefore not the precision of any single edge. It is the agreement of four differently motivated curves on roughly the same two depths.

chapters.title: The weakest test of content
chapters.body:
Excess [[kurtosis]] is the fourth standardized moment of a distribution minus three, so a Gaussian scores zero. The distribution here is the readout's logits over the whole vocabulary, at one position and one layer.

The mechanism is worth walking. A readout carrying nothing spreads its logits in a rough bell, with no token far from the bulk, and the fourth moment stays near its Gaussian value. A readout carrying something pushes a handful of tokens a long way into the tail. Because the fourth moment weights each deviation by its fourth power, those few tokens dominate the statistic.

So the measure rises with peakedness, and it does so without anyone deciding in advance which tokens would count as meaningful.

Pooled over a large set of activations, [[readout-excess-kurtosis]] is near zero through the first third of the depth, begins rising around a third of the way in, and falls in the last few layers.

This is the weakest question that can be put to a readout. It does not ask whether the top tokens are the right ones, or whether they name anything at all. It asks only that some tokens stand out from the rest.

A layer that fails it leaves nothing for the other statistics to find. That is what makes it the onset marker: the depth where it lifts off is the earliest point at which any claim about content can be made, and the band below it becomes the [[sensory-layers]] of the three-region division ([[layer-bands]]), where the [[j-space]] carries essentially no meaningful content.

The late fall is recorded but not leaned on; the end of the band is placed by other curves. And a peaked readout is a nonrandom readout, not yet one whose top tokens are [[verbalizable-representation|verbalizable content]]. Three more statistics follow for that reason.

chapters.title: Where the readout becomes the answer
chapters.body:
[[lens-next-token-accuracy]] scores agreement between the lens and the model's own output. At each position the lens produces a ranking over the vocabulary. The top $k$ of that ranking is taken, the model's actual top-1 prediction at that position is looked up, and the position counts as a hit if the prediction appears anywhere in the lens's top $k$. The score is the fraction of positions that hit.

That is a lenient test. The lens is not required to rank the token first, only to place it somewhere near the front.

The curve is near zero through most of the early layers, ticks up at the workspace start, rises slowly across the middle, and jumps steeply in the final few layers.

The slow middle rise is not read as an event. Layers do carry some information about what comes next, and more of it with depth. The steep jump is the event: from there the readout is no longer distinguishable from the model's [[next-token-prediction]].

The paper reads that as the end of the workspace proper. In those final layers the lens vectors act as [[motor-layers]] content driving the imminent output, rather than intermediate results still available to be read and combined further on. Availability is what the workspace claim turns on ([[llm-global-workspace-hypothesis]]), and a representation that is already the answer has nothing left to be available for.

The reasoning has a soft spot worth naming. Every layer moves toward the output, so a rise here is expected on any account of the model. What this curve fixes is the depth at which the lens stops separating a layer's content from the prediction — the same small late block already visible in the [[cka]] structure ([[fig-27]]). That the model changes regime there rests on the other curves turning at the same depth.

chapters.title: What survives a gap
chapters.body:
[[top1-autocorrelation]] asks whether the lens keeps saying the same thing as the text moves on. At a given layer, the top-1 readout token is recorded at every position of a document, and position $t$ is compared with position $t+\Delta$: how often the same token still holds the top slot after a gap of $\Delta$.

The raw rate would not mean much on its own. Some tokens sit at the top of lens readouts far more often than others, so two nearby positions can agree by coincidence rather than by carry-over.

The [[position-shuffled-null]] removes that. The same readouts are reassigned to shuffled positions, which leaves each token's overall frequency intact while destroying any genuine persistence. Panel c plots the difference in log probability between the real measurement and this null, so zero means no more repetition than chance produces.

The curve sits near the null in the early layers, rises at the same depth as the other metrics, peaks across the middle band, and falls back toward the null at the end.

This is the curve that matches most directly the property being claimed. Early content is the identity of the token at that position, which changes at every position. Late content is the token about to be produced, which also changes at every position. Content that survives a gap is content abstracted from both.

One curve therefore separates [[workspace-layers]] from both neighbours, using the same measurement at each end.

It shows persistence and nothing more. That the model actively moves such content between positions is a separate claim, supported later by the evidence for [[j-space-broadcast]] and for the [[broadcast-heads]] that carry it between positions.

chapters.title: The curve that rises twice
chapters.body:
[[j-space-effective-dimensionality]] is computed from the dictionary alone. The layer's lens vectors are collected, their variance is spread across the $d_{\text{model}}$ directions of the residual stream, and the statistic is the fraction of those directions needed to reach a fixed share of the total.

Early in the model that fraction is small. The whole dictionary lies in a thin subspace — whatever the lens vectors are at those depths, they nearly all point within a few directions.

The same low rank surfaces in a separate measurement, where early J-lens vectors are nearly orthogonal to those of the [[logit-lens]] and the [[tuned-lens]] ([[inter-lens-agreement]]). Rank keeps mattering after the onset too: the heads that relay workspace content concentrate in the first half of the band, where the effective rank is lowest ([[broadcast-head-layer-placement]]).

At the onset the fraction rises sharply, as the vectors fan out to span most of the residual stream.

Then it rises a second time, less dramatically, at the motor transition. This second rise is a different kind of fact.

$J_\ell$ maps a perturbation of the residual stream at layer $\ell$ to its effect at the final layer. Close to the output there is little computation left between the two, and the paper states that $J_\ell$ there approaches the identity ([[jacobian-approaches-identity]]). That makes $W_U J_\ell$ collapse toward $W_U$ itself: the lens has become the plain unembedding projection and inherits its full dimensionality.

So the late rise reports an instrument converging on a trivial limit, not a model spreading its content over more directions.

That cuts both ways. If the shape of this curve at one end is a property of the lens, the flat floor at the other end is a candidate for the same reading — which is the caveat recorded as [[early-layer-lens-degeneracy]].
